sources.title: Mekopa/whisperx-blackwell — WhisperX on GB10 via sm_121-to-sm_90 spoof
sources.summary: Prebuilt and buildable WhisperX (transcription + pyannote diarization) image for DGX Spark GB10 that works around missing prebuilt sm_121 PyTorch kernels by spoofing the reported compute capability.

facts.claim: The compatibility trick forces get_device_capability() to return (9,0) for SM_121, i.e. it reports the Blackwell GB10 GPU as Hopper SM_90 to PyTorch so existing sm_90 kernels run, because Blackwell can execute Hopper (SM_90) code natively.
facts.evidence: "Forces get_device_capability() to return (9, 0) for SM_121"; "Blackwell [is designed] to execute Hopper (SM_90) code natively."

facts.claim: Pre-built image available via `docker pull mekopa/whisperx-blackwell:latest`; source build via `docker build -f Dockerfile.gpu -t whisperx-blackwell:latest .`
Tested on PyTorch 2.6.0 inside NVIDIA container 25.01, CUDA 13.0.
facts.evidence: "PyTorch 2.6.0 (NVIDIA container 25.01)" with "CUDA 13.0"

facts.claim: Measured on a 24-minute audio file: CPU fallback ~2 hours vs GPU (patched) 62 seconds — about 115x speedup; the main win is enabling GPU speaker diarization (otherwise CPU-only).
facts.evidence: table: CPU Fallback ~2 hours — ; GPU (Patched) 62 seconds ~115x

sources.relevance_to_us: Direct, working recipe for the STT tier Steven wants to move off WindowsDesktop's Whisper :8001 onto DGX Spark: WhisperX (Whisper + diarization) with a documented sm_121 workaround and a real 115x GPU speedup number.

sources.title: Running whisper.cpp STT server on DGX Spark (GB10, ARM64 + CUDA 13) via Docker
sources.summary: NVIDIA developer forum thread with a working Docker recipe for building whisper.cpp's CUDA server on GB10/ARM64/CUDA 13, including the exact CMake architecture flags and several gotchas.

facts.claim: Correct CMake flag is CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="120;121" (not 121 alone) — building for plain 120 targets sm_120a which is not compatible with GB10.
facts.evidence: CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="120;121" ... "120 compiles for sm_120a which is not compatible"

facts.claim: Working Docker base image is nvidia/cuda:13.0.3-devel-ubuntu24.04, built with GGML_CUDA=ON and CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
Ubuntu 24.04 is required (not 22.04) because DGX OS ships GLIBC 2.38 and Ubuntu 22.04 containers only carry GLIBC 2.35.
facts.evidence: "The DGX OS ships with GLIBC 2.38; Ubuntu 22.04 containers only have GLIBC 2.35"

facts.claim: Gotchas hit: "CUDA error: no kernel image is available for execution on the device" when copying host-compiled binaries into a container; "libcuda.so.1 not found at build time" requiring CUDA stubs; and nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda has no ARM64 tags, so use nvidia/cuda from Docker Hub instead.
One user reports sub-second responses with large-v3-turbo and multi-language detection, but no formal RTF/latency benchmark numbers were posted in the thread.
facts.evidence: "sub-second responses with large-v3-turbo and multi-language support"

sources.relevance_to_us: The most directly reusable build recipe for whisper.cpp (or whisper NIM-adjacent CUDA build) on the exact GB10/CUDA 13/ARM64 target Steven's Spark will run — gives the CMake arch flag and base image without trial and error.

sources.title: NVML Support for DGX Spark Grace Blackwell Unified Memory — Community Solution
sources.summary: Community-built NVML shim (nvml-unified-shim) that replaces libnvidia-ml.so.1 to make GPU-memory-reading tools (pynvml, PyTorch/TensorFlow monitors, nvidia-smi wrappers, DGX Dashboard) work on GB10's unified memory, since the standard NVML memory query fails.

facts.claim: Root problem: NVML queries fail because GB10 uses unified memory architecture (128GB shared CPU+GPU) rather than a discrete GPU with dedicated framebuffer.

Fix: install via `git clone https://github.com/CINOAdam/nvml-unified-shim.git`, `make -f Makefile.python`, `sudo make -f Makefile.python install`. The shim implements 16 core NVML functions using the CUDA Runtime API plus /proc/meminfo for unified memory queries.
facts.evidence: "Uses CUDA Runtime API + /proc/meminfo for unified memory queries" ... "16 core NVML functions implemented"

facts.claim: With the shim: MAX Engine GPU detection, PyTorch/TensorFlow GPU monitoring, pynvml, nvidia-smi wrapper, and DGX Dashboard telemetry all work. Limitation: GPU utilization still reports 0% because traditional utilization metrics don't apply to unified memory systems.
facts.evidence: "0% since traditional metrics don't apply"

sources.relevance_to_us: Direct answer to the ch14 gap: the exact mechanism (and repo) for making GPU-memory metrics readable on GB10's unified memory for Prometheus/exporter/DGX-Dashboard integration, plus the known remaining limitation (utilization % unavailable).

sources.title: GPU plugin fails on DGX Spark (GB10) — nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo returns "Not Supported"
sources.summary: Kubernetes DRA driver bug report confirming nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo returns Not Supported on GB10, crashing the driver's GPU enumeration path (unlike the k8s-device-plugin which handles it gracefully).

facts.claim: nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo() returns "Not Supported" on GB10 (DGX Spark) because of the unified memory architecture, and this causes the DRA driver's GPU enumeration code to fail (unlike the standard NVIDIA k8s-device-plugin, which handles the same response gracefully).

sources.relevance_to_us: Confirms this is a known, filed compatibility issue across multiple NVIDIA k8s GPU tooling projects (DRA driver, HAMi, k8s-device-plugin) — relevant if Steven's k3d-with-GPU setup on the Spark (ch8) uses any of these device plugins for scheduling.

sources.title: Investigating Performance Issue/Bottleneck (DGX Spark forum)
sources.summary: Forum thread diagnosing low LLM inference throughput on DGX Spark; root-caused to using the Transformers library (inefficient) rather than a proper serving stack, plus fundamental memory-bandwidth limits on dense models.

facts.claim: User's raw benchmark: 14-20 tok/s on Llama 3B, ~10 tok/s on Llama 8B, using the Transformers library directly; power draw never exceeded ~25W and GPU utilization sat ~95% during these tests.
facts.evidence: "between 14 and 20 tokens/s running a llama 3B model and around 10 tokens/s for llama 8B"; "I've never seen power draw exceed ~25W"; "~95% gpu utilization during these benchmark tests"

facts.claim: Diagnosis: Transformers library is inefficient for inference (recommend vLLM, llama.cpp, or SGLang instead); decode phase is memory-bandwidth-bound at 273 GB/s LPDDR5X, making dense models inherently slower; better model choices are MoE-based (Qwen3, GPT-OSS, GLM) over Llama.
With correct framework/model choices, single-Spark systems reportedly reach 36-82 tok/s.
facts.evidence: "Single Spark systems showed 36-82 tokens/s with appropriate model/framework combinations"

sources.relevance_to_us: Real measured power figure under LLM load (~25W, ~95% GPU util) that contradicts naive assumptions of high power draw during inference — useful corroboration/contrast for the ch17 cost chapter's power-draw discussion, and reinforces ch6's framework-choice guidance (vLLM/SGLang over Transformers).

sources.title: Claude API / Claude Platform pricing (Anthropic docs)
sources.summary: Anthropic's current official pricing page (docs.anthropic.com/.../pricing redirects here). Full per-model $/MTok table, prompt caching multipliers, batch discount, and a worked-example cost calculation.

facts.claim: Claude Sonnet 5: $2/MTok base input, $2.50/MTok 5m cache write, $4/MTok 1h cache write, $0.20/MTok cache hit, $10/MTok output.
facts.evidence: table row "Claude Sonnet 5 | $2/MTok | $2.50/MTok | $4/MTok | $0.20/MTok | $10/MTok"

facts.claim: Claude Haiku 4.5: $1/MTok input, $1.25/MTok 5m cache write, $2/MTok 1h cache write, $0.10/MTok cache hit, $5/MTok output.
Claude Opus 5 / Opus 4.8: $5/MTok input, $25/MTok output (base rates); with Fast Mode research preview, both are billed at $10/MTok input, $50/MTok output across the full context window.
Prompt caching multipliers relative to base input price: 5-minute cache write = 1.25x, 1-hour cache write = 2x, cache read (hit) = 0.1x.
Batch API gives a 50% discount on both input and output tokens across all models (e.g. Sonnet 5 batch: $1/MTok input, $5/MTok output).

Web search costs $10 per 1,000 searches on top of standard token costs; web fetch has no additional charge beyond token costs for fetched content (average 10kB page ≈ 2,500 tokens, 100kB doc ≈ 25,000 tokens, 500kB PDF ≈ 125,000 tokens).

Worked example: a 1-hour Claude Managed Agents coding session on Opus 5 with 50,000 input + 15,000 output tokens costs $0.705 total (input $0.25 + output $0.375 + session runtime $0.08 at $0.08/session-hour); with 40,000 of the input tokens as cache reads, total drops to $0.525.
facts.evidence: worked-example table, totals $0.705 and $0.525

sources.relevance_to_us: Ground-truth current $/MTok figures for ch17's cost-control chapter — lets the guide compute real dollar examples for "what stays local (Whisper/embeddings on Spark) vs what spends Anthropic tokens (Claude Code / agentic loops)" instead of estimating.

sources.title: Manage costs effectively — Claude Code docs
sources.summary: Official Claude Code cost-management doc: enterprise average per-developer spend, /usage command output, background token usage, and concrete cost-reduction techniques (hooks, skills, subagents, model choice, context management).

facts.claim: Across enterprise deployments, average cost is around $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month, with 90% of users staying below $30/active day.
facts.evidence: "the average cost is around \$13 per developer per active day and \$150-250 per developer per month, with costs remaining below \$30 per active day for 90% of users"

facts.claim: Background token usage (conversation summarization for --resume, /usage status checks) typically costs under $0.04 per session even without active interaction.
facts.evidence: "typically under \$0.04 per session even without active interaction"

facts.claim: Agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode, because each teammate maintains its own context window and runs as a separate Claude instance.
facts.evidence: "Agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode"

facts.claim: Cost-reduction levers documented: /clear between unrelated tasks, moving detailed instructions from CLAUDE.md into on-demand skills (keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines), delegating verbose operations (test runs, log processing) to subagents so only a summary returns to the main context, PreToolUse hooks that filter noisy command output before it reaches context, and choosing Haiku for subagents / Sonnet for most coding / Opus for complex reasoning.

A cache miss (first message after a break longer than the cache lifetime) reprocesses the full context: cache lifetime is 1 hour on a subscription (5 min once drawing on usage credits, or settable back to 1h via ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1), and 5 minutes by default on an API key or cloud provider.

sources.relevance_to_us: Directly usable for ch17: gives the real $13/day, $150-250/month enterprise baseline (useful to contrast against local-inference cost avoidance on the Spark) plus concrete, sourced cost-control techniques (subagents, skills, hooks, model tiering) — this is exactly the multi-device, subagent-heavy workflow this research task itself is running under.

load_bearing_claims.claim: The correct CUDA build architecture flag for compiling GPU code (whisper.cpp and similar) for GB10 is CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="120;121" — NOT 120 alone, which targets the incompatible sm_120a.

load_bearing_claims.claim: nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo() returns 'Not Supported' on GB10 by design (unified memory has no discrete framebuffer), and the community fix is the nvml-unified-shim library, not a driver bug workaround.
load_bearing_claims.why_it_matters: This determines whether Steven's existing Prometheus/Grafana GPU dashboards will work unmodified on the Spark (they won't, without this shim or an equivalent) — directly shapes ch14's observability chapter and any k8s GPU-scheduling decisions in ch8/ch9.
